subject: Pharmacology
summary: NSAIDs are widely used for pain, fever and inflammation but carry risks of GI, renal and cardiovascular harm, especially in low‑resource settings where monitoring is limited.

sections.p: NSAIDs are drugs that inhibit cyclo‑oxygenase (COX) enzymes, reducing prostaglandin synthesis. They are identified by their therapeutic use and side‑effect profile rather than a single diagnostic test.
Adverse effects are graded by organ system involvement: mild (e.g., dyspepsia), moderate (gastric ulcer, renal impairment), severe (bleeding, acute kidney injury, myocardial infarction).
In East Africa, common precipitating factors include polypharmacy with antimalarials, HIV treatment, herbal remedies, and dehydration.
Patients may report abdominal pain, dyspepsia, nausea, or overt GI bleeding. Renal toxicity presents with oliguria or rising creatinine; cardiovascular events with chest pain or dyspnoea.
Baseline labs and monitoring are essential where available; otherwise clinical assessment guides management.

t.b: Detects anaemia from GI bleeding – anaemia indicates significant blood loss
Baseline renal function; rising values suggest AKI
Elevated transaminases may indicate hepatotoxicity or underlying hepatitis B
Hematuria or proteinuria signals renal injury
Detects perforation if available; otherwise clinical signs of peritonitis guide surgery

sections.p: Urgent care is needed for haematemesis, melena, oliguria, chest pain, or sudden drop in blood pressure.
Stop the offending NSAID, provide supportive care, and treat complications. Choice of alternative analgesic depends on comorbidities.
b: Paracetamol for pain/fever if no contraindication
COX‑2 selective agents avoided in cardio‑risk
Opioids only if necessary, with lowest effective dose

t.b: Prevents gastric ulcer in high‑risk patients
Treats dehydration and supports renal perfusion
Reduces bleeding in severe GI haemorrhage

sections.p: Educate patients on avoiding NSAIDs with known risks, monitor renal function if long‑term use is unavoidable, and use gastroprotection in high‑risk groups.
b: Avoid NSAIDs with ACE inhibitors or diuretics
Regularly review renal and hepatic function

sections.p: Other causes of abdominal pain and renal dysfunction can mimic NSAID toxicity.
In low‑resource settings, normal CBC may mask occult bleeding; creatinine may be normal until late AKI.
b: Low sensitivity of haemoglobin for GI bleed
Delayed rise in creatinine until 50% loss of function

faq.q: Why is aspirin still used in low‑resource settings?
faq.a: Its low cost and antiplatelet effect make it useful for secondary prevention of cardiovascular events, but it should be avoided in active GI disease.

faq.q: Can herbal remedies cause NSAID toxicity?
faq.a: Yes, many traditional preparations contain salicylates or COX inhibitors that can produce similar GI and renal side effects.

faq.q: What is the safest analgesic for a patient on an ACE inhibitor?
faq.a: Paracetamol is preferred; avoid NSAIDs as they blunt the antihypertensive effect and can worsen renal function.

exam: A 35‑year‑old woman on cotrimoxazole presents with epigastric pain and vomiting – what is the most likely cause? — NSAID‑induced gastric ulcer due to COX‑1 inhibition; consider stopping NSAID and starting PPI.
A 50‑year‑old man with hypertension on ACE inhibitor develops oliguria after starting ibuprofen – what is the next step? — Stop ibuprofen, give IV fluids, monitor creatinine.
A child with malaria on paracetamol develops sudden chest pain – what should you suspect? — Acute coronary syndrome; NSAIDs are contraindicated in malaria due to risk of renal impairment.
A patient with HIV on antiretroviral therapy reports abdominal pain after taking diclofenac – what is the differential? — GI ulcer, hepatitis B flare, drug‑drug interaction with protease inhibitors.
A 60‑year‑old with chronic kidney disease needs pain relief – which analgesic is safest? — Paracetamol; avoid NSAIDs and opioids unless necessary.
A patient on aspirin for stroke prevention develops melena – what is the management? — Stop aspirin, start PPI, consider endoscopy if bleeding persists.
A 28‑year‑old with sickle cell crisis takes ibuprofen for pain – what complication is most concerning? — Acute kidney injury due to dehydration and NSAID nephrotoxicity.
